item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Durante más de tres meses, los Yankees de Nueva York han planificado el regreso de Aaron Judge en torno a una idea: recuperar a su capitán para octubre sin exigirle que recupere de golpe los 99 días que se ha perdido.
Por eso su primera semana tras el regreso nunca pareció normal. Judge volvió sin haber pasado por una etapa de rehabilitación en las ligas menores. Los Yankees limitaron sus entradas, intercalaron descansos programados y consideraron los partidos de las Grandes Ligas como la fase final de su preparación. Solo jugó seis entradas en su regreso el 8 de septiembre y el martes tuvo un descanso programado tras disputar seis partidos seguidos.
Los Yankees estaban dispuestos a sacrificar el ritmo de septiembre a cambio de la forma física en octubre. Para este fin de semana en Arizona, se suponía que esa ecuación iba a cambiar. Judge ya había superado la fase de entrenamiento controlado. Nueva York se preparaba para aumentar su carga de trabajo y darle esos turnos al bate regulares que se había perdido durante su larga recuperación en la liga mayor.
La urgencia ya se notaba en los resultados. Judge tenía un promedio de 4 de 21 con 11 strikeouts en sus primeros seis partidos tras su reincorporación. Su jonrón de tres carreras del lunes en Minnesota fue la primera señal de que estaba dando la talla, pero no borró todos esos swings fallidos. Los Yankees necesitaban más práctica que otro reinicio.
Según la clasificación de la MLB, los Yankees tienen un balance de 88-64 al comenzar el viernes, a cinco partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con 10 partidos por disputar. Cuatro de ellos serán contra los Rays la semana que viene. La plaza para la postemporada está asegurada, pero Nueva York todavía tiene que prepararse para la lucha por el título de división y una posible serie de comodines.
Por eso, esta etapa no se centró tanto en demostrar que Judge podía volver, sino más bien en asegurarse de que pudiera volver a asumir la carga de trabajo habitual de octubre. Se suponía que cada partido le acercaría un poco más a su máximo rendimiento, le ayudaría a recuperar la sincronización frente a los lanzadores de las Grandes Ligas y eliminaría otra incertidumbre de cara a la postemporada. Se suponía que esa iba a ser la fase final y sin complicaciones del plan de los Yankees para octubre, antes de que empezara la postemporada.
El plan de puesta en marcha se ve interrumpido
En cambio, Judge llega a Arizona con una molestia en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha tras la derrota del miércoles por 5-4, en la 13.ª entrada, ante los Minnesota Twins en el Target Field. Notó el problema por primera vez en la primera entrada y siguió en el campo hasta que Heliot Ramos entró como bateador suplente en su lugar en la sexta.
Era su séptimo partido desde que volvió tras una fractura por estrés en la costilla derecha, después de 99 días de baja. Con esos dos strikeouts, su promedio desde que volvió queda en 4 de 23, con 13 strikeouts y un jonrón.
Judge dijo que intentó seguir jugando antes de que él y el entrenador Aaron Boone decidieran que el riesgo para los Yankees era mayor que lo que valía seguir en el campo.
«Intenté seguir jugando a ver hasta dónde podía llegar, porque estos partidos son importantes en esta recta final», dijo Judge. «Lo hablé con los míos y pensamos que sería lo mejor para no perjudicar al equipo, ni en el campo ni en las bases».
Los Yankees tuvieron el jueves libre para someterse a tratamiento. A primera hora del viernes, la MLB seguía indicando que tenía una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha, sin fecha de regreso.
David Cone señala un problema aún mayor para octubre
La primera cuestión es la disponibilidad. La más importante es la preparación.
El analista de YES Network, David Cone, se centró en eso el jueves. Judge ha tenido 24 turnos al bate desde que volvió, y 13 de ellos han acabado en strikeouts.
«Estoy preocupado», dijo Cone. «Necesita turnos al bate… Tiene un problema en la parte inferior de la pierna, en la pantorrilla. Simplemente no lo sabemos. No lo sabremos hasta que sepamos qué tan grave es. ¿Va a tener más turnos al bate antes de que acabe la temporada regular? Ahora mismo es una auténtica incógnita».
Ahora, el hecho de haberse saltado la fase de rehabilitación cobra más importancia. El exreceptor All-Star A.J. Pierzynski dijo que una temporada en las ligas menores podría haberle proporcionado un entorno menos exigente para lidiar con las molestias tras una larga ausencia.
«Por eso te vas de rehabilitación, sobre todo cuando has estado tanto tiempo de baja como Aaron Judge. Él mismo lo ha dicho: esto es como los entrenamientos de primavera, así que intentas quitarte de encima las molestias y otras cosillas que surgen yendo de rehabilitación», dijo Pierzynski. «Él no lo hizo, no quiso hacerlo».
Nadie puede saber si una asignación a la rehabilitación habría evitado esa tensión en la pierna. Los Yankees ahora corren el riesgo de que Judge pierda más turnos al bate que aún necesita.
El equilibrio de los pelotones no es el problema
Una comparación actual del OPS de los Yankees y los Red Sox destaca a Judge, Ben Rice y Cody Bellinger como bateadores de Nueva York que rinden bien contra cualquiera de los dos equipos. Según Baseball Savant, Judge tiene un OPS de 0,839 contra lanzadores diestros y de 0,892 contra zurdos. Bellinger tiene unas cifras casi idénticas: 0,794 y 0,795. Rice tiene un OPS de 0,937 contra lanzadores diestros y de 0,784 contra zurdos.
Judge no necesita un papel de bateador de reserva. Los Yankees necesitan que esté listo para batear regularmente contra cualquier rival.
Judge tiene un promedio de bateo de .241/.360/.511, con 18 jonrones y 41 carreras impulsadas en 66 partidos. La cuestión es si los Yankees podrán recuperar el ritmo de juego suficiente antes de octubre.
El plazo de la Liga Internacional convierte la precaución en una apuesta con la plantilla
Si los Yankees metieran a Judge en la lista de lesionados ahora, no podría jugar hasta el partido 161, lo que le dejaría, como mucho, el último partido de la temporada regular para ponerse a punto.
Si los Yankees creen que puede volver antes, pueden mantenerlo en la plantilla y jugar temporalmente con un jugador menos disponible en la plantilla de 28.
Jasson Domínguez y Max Schuemann figuraban ambos en la alineación del equipo de Triple A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre el jueves, lo que sugiere que no habrá ningún sustituto inmediato.
Esto deja a Nueva York ante la disyuntiva que intentó evitar durante el primer regreso de Judge: proteger su físico o proteger su preparación. A falta de 10 partidos, puede que los Yankees no tengan tiempo suficiente para hacer ambas cosas a fondo.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.content:encoded:
Will Yankees' postseason first-timers prove to be ready for the moment?
This browser does not support the video element.
It’s common to think of the Yankees as a playoff-tested team. After all, this is the eighth time in nine years that they’ve made the postseason under manager Aaron Boone. And a quick look at some of their regulars shows a lineup that varies between a little bit and a wealth of October experience.
Player No. of Career Playoff Games
Cody Bellinger 76
Aaron Judge 65
Paul Goldschmidt 29
Trent Grisham 26
Jazz Chisholm, Jr. 24
Austin Wells 21
Anthony Volpe 21
Amed Rosario 11
Ryan McMahon 10
Ben Rice 6
José Caballero 3
But a few names are missing from that list: Shortstop George Lombard Jr., outfielder Spencer Jones, first baseman Luis García Jr. and outfielder Heliot Ramos. Those four have never played in the postseason, either with the Yankees or -- as is the case with García and Ramos -- with their previous teams.
Now, it’s possible that some of the injured veteran players -- Grisham and Chisholm, specifically -- could return to the lineup and send some of those new faces to the bench or off the playoff roster entirely. But it’s safe to say the Yankees are going to be counting on at least a few playoff newbies next month in their quest to win their first World Series since 2009.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said his youngsters and playoff newcomers have another advantage over players who are coming of age in other markets.
“You play for the Yankees, you play in New York,” he said, “it has a way of getting you ready for the postseason.”
This browser does not support the video element.
But a few names are missing from that list: Shortstop George Lombard Jr., outfielder Spencer Jones, first baseman Luis García Jr. and outfielder Heliot Ramos. Those four have never played in the postseason, either with the Yankees or -- as is the case with García and Ramos -- with their previous teams.
Now, it’s possible that some of the injured veteran players -- Grisham and Chisholm, specifically -- could return to the lineup and send some of those new faces to the bench or off the playoff roster entirely. But it’s safe to say the Yankees are going to be counting on at least a few playoff newbies next month in their quest to win their first World Series since 2009.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said his youngsters and playoff newcomers have another advantage over players who are coming of age in other markets.
“You play for the Yankees, you play in New York,” he said, “it has a way of getting you ready for the postseason.”
This has been something of a transitional year in the Major Leagues. Check out the first round of the 2023 Draft if you want proof. No fewer than 19 of the 37 first-round and sandwich picks have debuted, and many of them are already impact players with their teams.
“Players are getting to the big leagues at a very quick pace now and at a young age,” said Tigers manager A.J. Hinch, who has welcomed No. 3 pick Max Clark and AL Rookie of the Year favorite Kevin McGonigle to Detroit this year. “I don't think they're as wowed by the big steps that they're taking.”
For the Yankees, that class includes Lombard, who has acclimated nicely since being called up in early August. And Jones was recently lauded by none other than Aaron Judge, who said the rookie outfielder has “really evolved every single time he got called up, gotten a little bit better and a little bit better.”
Of course, there will be hiccups along the way. On Wednesday, Jones went 0-for-6 with five strikeouts and committed an error when he dropped a fly ball in center field. And Lombard couldn’t come up with a Victor Caratini grounder in the 13th that was ruled a single as the Twins walked off the Yankees.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] New York Yankees Urged to Make Bold Paul Goldschmidt Decision
item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: The New York Yankees, much like all the other postseason teams in MLB, will have to make tough decisions when it comes to their October roster. It's a 26-man roster in October across MLB, and no team can carry more than 13 pitchers. How a club opts to round out its roster is entirely up to them, but speaking to the New York Yankees, a recent postseason projection leaves players like Paul Goldschmidt on the fringe. So, what should the Yankees do with their playoff roster, and who needs to be left
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees, much like all the other postseason teams in MLB, will have to make tough decisions when it comes to their October roster.
It's a 26-man roster in October across MLB, and no team can carry more than 13 pitchers. How a club opts to round out its roster is entirely up to them, but speaking to the New York Yankees, a recent postseason projection leaves players like Paul Goldschmidt on the fringe.
So, what should the Yankees do with their playoff roster, and who needs to be left off?
More MLB on Heavy: MLB World Reacts to George Lombard Jr. Blunder in Yankees-Twins Game
Yankees Urged to Dump Paul Goldschmidt from Playoff Roster
In a recent piece for FanSided.com, writer Jake Elman predicts a handful of Yankees players who could be dumped from the postseason roster, and Goldschmidt's name pops up:
"Let's get back to the present. Goldschmidt is hitting just .239 with a .680 OPS in 103 second-half plate appearances, and he's only capable of playing first or DHing. Ben Rice fills both roles, and Cody Bellinger can also play first if needed. The one thing potentially working in Goldschmidt's favor is his .313 average and 1.006 OPS against lefties, but that's not enough to warrant a roster spot in our eyes. Sorry, Goldy. At least you'd finally earn a World Series ring if the Yankees finish the job."
Paul Goldschmidt has been somewhat of a solid contributor for the Yankees this season, playing in 101 games and clubbing 18 home runs and 12 doubles, so his playoff status is certainly up for debate at this moment.
After all, not every team has a lefty masher like Goldy who would certainly be used purely as a platoon.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce 2 Roster Moves Before Reds Game
Should Paul Goldschmidt Make the Yankees Playoff Roster?
It's obviously all speculation on behalf of Elman, but he does bring up a big crossroads the Yankees will be at when it comes to a Goldschmidt decision.
The 39-year-old Goldy is also batting .253 this season with an OPS+ of 113, so he's an above-average hitter by 13% in MLB, against both righties and lefties.
Good thing I am not in the position to be making decisions like this, but Yankees fans, comment below what you would do with Paul Goldschmidt this October? And would he be part of your ideal Yankees batting order?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Sequence of the Week: Max Fried (9/15)
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody

item.content:encoded:
It wouldn't have been a proper Yankees-Twins series in Minnesota without a game that devolved into extra-innings madness. The Yankees failed to cash in multiple bases loaded opportunities and so missed a chance to sweep, falling farther behind the Rays in the standings. Nonetheless, the Bombers took care of business in the first two games of the series, and it is from the middle game that we pull our candidate for Sequence of the Week.
We join Max Fried with two outs in the bottom of the fifth on Tuesday at Target Field. The Yankees have a 3-1 lead courtesy of a Cody Bellinger two-run homer and George Lombard Jr. RBI single. However, the Twins are threatening to cut the lead to one with Emmanuel Rodriguez on second with a two-out double. That brings the number nine hitter Austin Martin to the plate, a batter Fried absolutely wants to retire to avoid the lineup turning over with a runner in scoring position.
After going almost all fastballs the first time he faced Martin, Fried looks to steal a called first-pitch strike with a backdoor sweeper.
After seeing mostly hard stuff that moved away from him, you can understand why Martin would give up on this pitch early given how far from the strike zone it is initially aimed. Fried sweeps in a dandy on the outer half for called strike one.
Establishing that backdoor breaking ball for a called strike forces Martin to respect any pitches that start away, even those that look like balls out of the hand. This opens up a host of possibilities for Fried, including the changeup low and away for chase.
This is a pretty well-executed changeup out of the zone down and outside. It looks like it is aimed at that corner of the zone before fading away from the hitter. You can see Martin was initially tempted to chase the pitch — a product of that first pitch backdoor sweeper — before holding up for an impressively disciplined take.
With Martin taking against that last pitch away, Fried and Ali Sánchez feel that there is an opening for another backdoor sweeper.
Another decently executed pitch, just a little too low to nip the bottom of the zone for a second called strike. It is worth noting that Martin showed some willingness to offer before backing off, so that outside pitch is still open for chase opportunities.
Not wanting to fall any further behind in the count, Fried throws his first fastball of the encounter. However, unlike the four-seamers and sinkers he threw Martin in the first AB, this cutter breaks toward the hitter instead of away. Therefore, if the hitter succeeds in reading fastball spin out of the hand, a backdoor cutter that starts off the plate away should freeze Martin.
That is precisely what happens, Fried pinpointing this cutter with precision on the corner up and away. Martin leaves the bat on his shoulder, only to watch the pitch cut across the black of the plate for called strike two.
Now that he has established his fastball in the zone and has the count leverage in his favor, Fried has an opening to climb the ladder with the cutter hoping for a chase and whiff under a pitch elevated above the zone.
Even though this offering misses the top of the zone by about a foot, it's not a complete waste pitch. Fried has reset the hitter's eye level for the fastball up, which should open the door for a breaking ball down and in.
That is just what Fried's thought process is with the count full. He doesn't need to give in with a fastball with first base open, knowing that it will be very hard for Martin to lay off a breaking ball that looks like a strike out of the hand.
Now this is what you call a back-foot sweeper. The pitch looks like a strike for much of its journey toward home until the lateral sweep really seems to accelerate in the final 15 feet. It's just where you want to land a pitch like this, close enough to the strike zone to extract the chase but close enough to the batter that he is not able to pull in his hands in time to make contact.
Here's the full sequence:
Asked after the start what positives he would take away, Fried cited breaking ball command and an economical pitch count to go seven strong on just 88 pitches, the first point certainly highlighted by this sequence.
The Yankees desperately needed this start from Fried, not only to boost their chances of winning this particular game but also as a sign of continued build-up from the recurrence of his left elbow bone bruise. Fried labored in the start before this one, needing 80 pitches to complete 3.1 innings. Seeing him back to his best when it comes to pitch efficiency and damage limitation has to be encouraging as they formulate their postseason rotation plans.

item.content:encoded:
Cody Bellinger es un jardinero zurdo nacido en Scottsdale que ha sido pieza clave en varios equipos de las Grandes Ligas. Con un debut en 2017 y una carrera marcada por altibajos, el jugador de los New York Yankees mantiene un promedio de .276 en 2026 con 16 jonrones y 71 carreras impulsadas, demostrando que sigue siendo un bate confiable en la alineación.
Orígenes
Nacido el 13 de julio de 1995 en Scottsdale, Arizona, Cody Bellinger creció en una familia de atletas y desarrolló su swing zurdo desde joven. Su camino hacia las Grandes Ligas fue rápido: debutó el 25 de abril de 2017, cuando apenas tenía 21 años, mostrando desde el principio la capacidad ofensiva que lo caracterizaría.
Los Los Angeles Dodgers fueron su primer hogar en la MLB, donde se consolidó como un talento emergente. Su versatilidad defensiva en el jardín izquierdo y su capacidad para conectar jonrones lo convirtieron en un prospect valioso desde sus primeras temporadas.
Carrera profesional
Bellinger alcanzó su mejor momento con los Dodgers en 2019, cuando ganó el Premio MVP de la Liga Nacional con números espectaculares. Esa fue la cumbre de su carrera individual, aunque sus contribuciones ofensivas se han mantenido consistentes a lo largo de los años.
Su trayectoria lo llevó posteriormente a los Chicago Cubs (2024: .266 AVG, 18 HR, 78 CI, OPS .751) antes de llegar a los New York Yankees. En 2025 mostró un repunte significativo con .272 de promedio, 29 jonrones y 98 carreras impulsadas en un OPS de .814, consolidándose como un bateador productivo en la alineación neoyorquina.
En 2026 mantiene un desempeño sólido con .276 de AVG, 16 HR y 71 CI en 71 carreras anotadas, además de 12 bases robadas. Su versatilidad y experiencia lo hacen un activo valioso para los Yankees en su búsqueda de un campeonato.
Estadísticas destacadas
| Temporada | AVG | HR | CI | R | OPS | SB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 New York Yankees | .276 | 16 | 71 | 71 | .795 | 12 |
| 2025 New York Yankees | .272 | 29 | 98 | 89 | .814 | 13 |
| 2024 Chicago Cubs | .266 | 18 | 78 | 72 | .751 | 9 |
Premios y récords
El mayor logro de Cody Bellinger fue ganar el MVP de la Liga Nacional en 2019, temporada en la que lideró varias categorías ofensivas. Además, fue parte del equipo de los Los Angeles Dodgers que ganó la Serie Mundial en 2020, contribuyendo en los playoffs con su defensa y su bate en momentos clave.
A lo largo de su carrera ha sido seleccionado para Juegos de Estrellas y ha recibido reconocimiento por su versatilidad defensiva, aunque su consistencia ofensiva ha fluctuado en los últimos años.
Dato curioso
Cody Bellinger proviene de una familia atlética: su padre, Mike Bellinger, fue jugador de béisbol profesional, lo que influyó en su formación desde pequeño. Su capacidad para adaptarse a diferentes roles en el jardín y su mentalidad competitiva lo han mantenido vigente en las Grandes Ligas incluso después de las lesiones y los cambios de equipo que marcaron su carrera a mitad de la década de 2020.
Últimas noticias de Cody Bellinger
Sigue la cobertura de Cody Bellinger en El Fildeo.

item.title: [FanSided] Yankees who clinched a playoff spot but could be dumped from the postseason roster

item.content:encoded:
For their sake, the New York Yankees better hope that superstar outfielder Aaron Judge’s newest injury is only a minor setback.
Judge left Wednesday’s extra-inning loss to the Twins with lower leg tightness, immediately raising concerns among fans that he’ll miss the Yankees’ first playoff series. New York entered play on Sept. 17 in firm control of the AL’s top Wild Card seed, putting them on track to host the No. 5 Red Sox in the first round.
If Judge can’t go when the playoffs begin on Sept. 29, then he won’t be the only notable contributor not in uniform during the Wild Card Series. Each team gets 26 players for their playoff rosters, but no more than 13 pitchers. Some clubs opt for 14 position players and 12 pitchers, though we personally prefer a 13-and-13 balance. Additionally, teams can adjust their rosters between series, and obviously they can replace an injured player if needed.
For this list, we’re only including players who are healthy and active as of Sept. 17. In other words, that means Trent Grisham, Giancarlo Stanton, and Ryan Weathers are among those who didn’t qualify. We’ve also omitted Judge because the Yankees haven’t announced the severity of his left leg injury.
Jasson Domínguez, OF
The writing has long been on the wall for Domínguez, who was recently demoted to Triple-A amid another disappointing season. Even if Judge potentially misses the Wild Card Round, it’s difficult to envision the 23-year-old Domínguez returning as a backup outfielder.
Frankly, the entire situation is unfortunate, because neither Domínguez’s talent nor his work ethic has been the issue. He’s always earned rave reviews for his maturity and overall attitude, but injuries — most notably to his elbow and shoulder — have seemingly sapped him of his once-potent power stroke.
Luis Gil, P
Gil has had an odd career, winning AL Rookie of the Year in 2024 despite debuting three years earlier. Injuries have limited him to a 3.92 ERA over 80.1 innings since the start of 2025, and he recently moved to the bullpen. We’ll see whether the Yankees view the 28-year-old as a long-term reliever, or if they’d bring him to spring training as a starter.
But for now, Gil is on the roster bubble, and we don’t expect him to crack the 26-man playoff squad. Clarke Schmidt’s return gives the Yankees another depth arm, and Gil hasn’t shown that he’s worth carrying on a limited staff. That said, we imagine he’d be among the first names called if injuries strike his teammates.
Paul Goldschmidt, 1B/DH
Goldschmidt turned 39 last week, and it’s unclear whether he’s in the final weeks of a likely Hall of Fame career. He’s totaled 65.3 bWAR, and the majority of the 142 players above him are already in the Hall of Fame or will be when they’re eligible.
Let’s get back to the present. Goldschmidt is hitting just .239 with a .680 OPS in 103 second-half plate appearances, and he’s only capable of playing first or DHing. Ben Rice fills both roles, and Cody Bellinger can also play first if needed.
The one thing potentially working in Goldschmidt’s favor is his .313 average and 1.006 OPS against lefties, but that’s not enough to warrant a roster spot in our eyes. Sorry, Goldy. At least you’d finally earn a World Series ring if the Yankees finish the job.
Will Warren, SP
This might come as a surprise, given that we included Warren in our most recent playoff roster projection. But the more that we think about things, Schmidt’s return feels like a significant blow to Warren’s chances of pitching in October. Do the Yankees really need two long relievers capable of eating up innings if the starter leaves early?
We initially had veteran swingman Ryan Yarbrough in this spot, though he might have the advantage as a left-handed reliever.. He also has a 2.91 ERA in 21.2 second-half innings and has since recovered from a lingering right oblique problem.

item.content:encoded:
Yahoo Sports: As you likely know by now, Aaron Judge exited yesterday's game early when Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him in the sixth. The Yankees announced it midgame as "lower leg tightness." It's some relief I suppose that Judge didn't re-aggravate the rib fracture that kept him out for over three months, and Judge himself downplayed the seriousness of the ailment after the game.
"We're still trying to ramp up so there's still going to be little things like this that come up," Judge said after the Yankees 13-inning loss to the Twins. "I just thought it would be best instead of pushing through it like I normally do." Judge seemed to view his exit from the game as precautionary, and likened it to the type of thing that would happen in spring training when small, nagging things pop up as players get back into playing shape.
MLB.com | Patrick Donnelly: Clarke Schmidt came off the 60-day injured list yesterday, something we saw coming; he allowed two hits but got two strikeouts while facing four batters in his first MLB action since July 3, 2025. What we didn't see coming was who was pushed off the roster to make room for Schmidt: fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera. The utilityman Cabrera had spent most of the year at Triple-A, hitting .288 with 19 homers and a .790 OPS, but hasn't spent much time with the big club ever since suffering a brutal ankle injury in a play at home plate last May. Cabrera seems likely to be claimed on waivers, meaning his time in the Bronx is likely to come to an end after being a member of the organization since signing at age-16 in July 2015.
The Athletic | Brendan Kuty: ($) Spencer Jones has been a bit of a revelation for the Yankees this year, producing at a high level across the outfield throughout the summer. He's benefited from shadowing another big lefty swinger in the outfield: Cody Bellinger. Bellinger is only 31, but has a very long and decorated track record for a player his age, something Jones has tried to tap into during his time with the Yankees. "As a young guy, I can't help but watch every time he's up there," Jones said of Bellinger. "When we are in the dugout," Jones said, "he's one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, 'Yo, what did you see?' He'll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he's going to do next time."
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Ryan Weathers cleared a key hurdle in his rehab earlier this week, tossing 15 pitches in a bullpen session and sitting 87-90 mph on his fastball. The hope, if things go right, is for the lefty to get into game action before the regular season ends. It's a tight timeline, but with Weathers set to throw another bullpen on Friday before perhaps facing live hitters early next week, it's doable. The Yankees could certainly use his arm in the bullpen as they try to sort out what their playoff relief corps will look like.
FanGraphs | Davy Andrews: This here isn't news, but it is fun. Andrews discusses the Amazon TV show Reacher, in which the titular character tries to maintain a low profile by checking into hotels under aliases, which are always Yankees second basemen. The problem, of course, is that Reacher's cover is often blown, because Yankee second basemen are frequently famous people with recognizable names (don't choose "Starlin Castro" as your alias if you're trying not to attract attention!). So, Andrews endeavors to help Reacher by finding players who played second base for the Yankees who would help Reacher stay undercover. Good aliases include second basemen from New York's Higlander days, like Joe Ward, and Otis Johnson. The worst possible aliases Andrews found? Robinson Canó and Mickey Mantle.

The veteran outfielder did what he could to set the table for the rest of the Yankees' lineup out of the two-hole, but offense got tough to find after Aaron Judge (lower leg) left the game in the sixth inning. item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, the New York Yankees are playing the finale of their three-game series against the Twins (in Minnesota).
They have won each of the first two games, so they are looking to go for a sweep.
Cody Bellinger started the game in left field (and hit second in the order).
Underdog MLB wrote: “Yankees 9/16 B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF A. Judge RF L. García Jr. 1B S. Jones CF G. Lombard Jr. SS R. McMahon 3B A. Wells C A. Volpe 2B C. Rodón SP”
UPDATE: The Yankees lost 5-4 on Wednesday.
Bellinger had three hits, one walk and one stolen base.
Yankees Make Sudden Cody Bellinger Change
During the game, the Yankees made a handful of lineup adjustments.
Bellinger was moved to first base.
The former MVP is arguably the best fielder on the team (and is very versatile).
He has been moved to first base several times this year, but only started there one time.
Looking At Bellinger
Bellinger is in the middle of his second season playing for the Yankees.
Prior to New York, the 2020 World Series Champion had stints with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Chicago Cubs.
He came into the day batting .272 with 126 hits, 16 home runs, 71 RBIs, 70 runs and 11 stolen bases in 124 games.
This year, Bellinger made his first All-Star Game appearance since 2019 (when he was with the Dodgers).
He also won the 2026 MLB All-Star Game MVP Award.
Looking At The Yankees Right Now
The Yankees are currently the second-place team in the American League East with an 88-63 record in 151 games.
They are just 3.5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for first.
Following their series with the Twins, the Yankees will head to Arizona to face off against the Diamondbacks on Friday night.

item.content:encoded:
It's been a nice start to the week in the Yankees' home-away-from-home. On Monday night, they clinched a postseason berth with a 7-3 win against the Twins. On Tuesday evening, they fielded the proverbial "hangover lineup" of sorts and still cruised to an 8-1 victory behind a strong start from Max Fried and plenty of strong performances at the plate.
On today's getaway day game in Minneapolis, Carlos Rodón leads the Yankees' effort for a sweep. His most recent start against the Mets was perhaps the best of his season, as he held down the crosstown rivals for one run in 6.1 innings—with eight strikeouts to just one walk. For Rodón, who has for various reasons not pitched deep into games as routinely as he did in 2025, a second straight start of six or more innings would be an excellent sign as he prepares for the postseason.
The Twins, now 4-9 in September, will look to young righty Zebby Matthews, who has turned in an uneven campaign on the hill this season. His past three starts have been illustrative of the step-forward-step-back tendency which has tormented many a young hurler. On August 30th, he twirled an absolute gem, pitching into the ninth inning against the rival White Sox with just one run allowed in a win. His next appearance, also against Chicago, was a far more pedestrian five-inning, four-run effort. Then last time out, he failed to escape the third inning in Detroit—walking four batters and surrendering five runs to hit the showers early.
While the Yankees rested a few of their starters for last night's contest, including Aaron Judge, it didn't prevent them from running up the score. Today, Judge returns to the lineup card, hitting third behind DH Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, who led the way with three hits and a homer last night. Cleanup hitter Luis García Jr., Spencer Jones, and George Lombard Jr. will make up the middle of the order, with Ryan McMahon, Austin Wells, and second baseman Anthony Volpe (it's still weird to say that) pulling up the rear.
How to watch
Location: Target Field, Minneapolis, MN
First pitch: 1:40 pm ET
TV broadcast: YES, Twins.TV
Radio broadcast: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 (NYY), TIBN, The Wolf 102.9 FM, LosTwins.com (MIN)
Online stream: MLB.tv (out-of-market only), Gotham Sports App

item.title: [roundtable.io] Cody Bellinger's Resurgence Means Everything to the Yankees
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: The resurgence of Cody Bellinger has been key in the New York Yankees' recent push. For a while there, New York Yankees outfielder Cody Bellinger was completely dormant offensively. item.content:encoded:
The resurgence of Cody Bellinger has been key in the New York Yankees' recent push.
For a while there, New York Yankees outfielder Cody Bellinger was completely dormant offensively. Between July and August, Bellinger managed just one home run and 10 RBI, and while he missed time with a hamstring injury, he wasn't effective even when he was healthy.
Bellinger posted a sub-.700 OPS for three straight months heading into September, and it was beginning to look like one of those years for the former NL MVP. This even though he got off to a torrid start this season.
But since the calendar flipped to September, Bellinger looks like a different hitter.
The lefty slugger is slashing .370/.375/.648 with four homers and 12 RBI over 56 plate appearances through the first half of the month, most recently going 3-for-4 with a two-run blast against the Minnesota Twins on Tuesday night.
Has Bellinger's resurgence coincided with the return of Aaron Judge? Somewhat. Judge came back on Sept. 8, and since then, Bellinger has mashed four long balls and has a hit in all but one game.
However, Bellinger was also rolling the first week of September, and Judge was not in the lineup when Bellinger smacked his two-run homer Tuesday evening.
There is no question that Bellinger's dip in production was largely a result of both Judge and Giancarlo Stanton being sidelined. The 31-year-old is no longer the player he was from his early Los Angeles Dodgers days when he could carry a lineup. He need support.
But when he gets it, he becomes incredibly valuable.
Bellinger is slashing .272/.347/.443 with 16 home runs and 71 RBI over 527 plate appearances on the campaign. Has he been quite as good as last year when he smashed 29 dingers while posting an .813 OPS? No, and we cannot ignore just how invisible he was for such a long stretch when the Yankees desperately needed him to produce.
But the $162.5 million man is getting hot at the right time, with the MLB playoffs starting in less than two weeks. And we know just how outstanding he is in he field, as Bellinger has posted an incredible 19 defensive runs saved and six outs above average in 2026.
Hopefully, Bellinger can sustain his recent surge heading into the postseason, especially considering it appears that Stanton will remain on the shelf.
The Yankees paid Bellinger like an All-Star. That requires hitting like one. We'll see if it can continue.

item.content:encoded:
All Micah Franklin ever did was hit. In the minor leagues, MLB, KBO, and NPB, it didn’t matter. After a career of waiting for his shot, he translated all the base hits he kept in storage into Cody Bellinger’s bat.
When Franklin learned on the fly through the professional ranks, teaching hitting looked very different.
“It was a little different back in the olden days, as we call them,” Franklin said with a chuckle. “We didn’t have a hitting coach.”
Franklin and his teammates depended on the “hitting coordinator,” who came around once or twice a season. Traditionally considered a grind, minor league baseball has since seen legitimate facilities and pay structure upgrades. In contrast, during Franklin’s time, they made the most of what they had.
“I didn’t have a cage until my second year in Triple-A. By then, I think I was in the fifth year of my minor league career,” he said. “We had tees, and then sometimes we would soft toss to each other against the chain-link fence. You know, this was minor league ball. So you had to figure out what you were doing in a game.”
Still, the challenging environment was no match for Franklin’s blistering bat. Across a substantial sample of 1,141 minor league games, he posted an .866 OPS, mashed 200 home runs, and had more than 1,000 hits.
His success carried overseas when he played in Korea and Japan, posting an OPS of .887 across four seasons.
It’s no surprise Franklin was such a consistent offensive threat because one of his mentors was the always docile, yet superlative Willie McGee.
“I met Willie McGee at 19. In the offseason, I got a lot of work in with him; we would go 500 swings a day. No coaching, really, just talking about different things and how to hit the ball,” Franklin said.
“It was more like, ‘Hey, stay inside the ball. Let’s go the other way.’ You’d start left-handed. The first 25 swings the other way, then 25 swings up the middle, left-center; 25 swings; 25 line drives up the middle; 25 line drives right-center. Then you go right-handed and reverse it. Now, if you hit a pop-up or roll over, you don’t count that. Your concentration is on the task, so you’re hitting line drives. You’re not trying to hit the ball as hard and far as you can. You’re trying to have bat control and body control that way.”
Franklin implements the skills he acquired as a successful professional player in his post-pro career as a hitting coach.
As a coach, Franklin emphasizes a program he’s titled “7 to 22.” The approach is simple: If you attack the ball between 7 and 22 degrees, it creates a bat path that promotes consistency and builds a steady foundation for success.
Some see Franklin’s philosophy and assume he’s created a cookie-cutter mentality for all hitters. In reality, it’s anything but.
“I do not teach hitting one way,” Franklin said. “A lot of people will say, ‘Yeah, you do,’ but no. Actually, I don’t.”
Due to his knack for adaptation, Franklin experiments with all kinds of tools and approaches. His experience around the game has led him to a conclusion about all the tech craze surrounding modern baseball.
“I don’t think there are any, in my opinion, advantages of the new technology,” he said. “That’s with me going all in on the new technology, learning, getting educated from body movement to caveats to all this scientific stuff. Because even when I was all in on it and teaching it, I realized that it is hampering the kid. It’s putting a crutch. These kids don’t know how to do anything else now.”
The quick adjustments he learned to make during his own playing days seem to have become a lost art. Kids are struggling to make them, and it’s a trickle-up effect that’s even left some MLB hitters guessing.
“I changed all the time, and within the at-bat, I changed depending on that type of pitcher,” he said. “What got me quicker to the ball or quicker to what I wanted to do in that situation? So I changed my approach, my thinking, so much. In today’s game, kids don’t know how to change enough.”
One of those kids was Cody Bellinger.
Bellinger came up with the Los Angeles Dodgers and had a riveting start to his MLB career.
Over his first three seasons, from 2017 to 2019, he earned a Rookie of the Year, an MVP, two All-Star selections, a Gold Glove, a Silver Slugger, and 17.2 bWAR. It was a start that seemed almost too good to be true.
Then 2020 happened: masks, disease, isolation, and fever dreams. But there was still baseball.
Unfortunately for Bellinger, it wasn’t the same brand he anticipated. His OPS dipped to a then-career-low .789 in the shortened season. Although the Dodgers won a World Series, casting the best kind of shadow over his dormant year, cracks were beginning to show.
2021 solidified the regressive state, as Bellinger’s -1.6 bWAR was among MLB’s worst. Pair that with a sub-.600 OPS, and he had entered career-threatening territory.
This steep and puzzling drop-off left most of MLB questioning the root cause.
Franklin wasn’t confused at all. He knew exactly what to do.
Long before Bellinger was hitting “Belli-bombs” at Chavez Ravine, he was just a kid in the desert, playing on a scout team that Franklin assembled.
“Mike Fedders and I, we put a whole book together for the D-backs because we weren’t drafting local kids. We’re like, ‘What the hell? There are all these local kids here. How come we aren’t drafting them and other teams are?’
“Well, they paid for a scout team for two years. And this scout team was handpicked, so it wasn’t like a traditional scout team. The D-backs paid, and they said, ‘Go and find players.’ So I did.”
That’s where Franklin met Bellinger.
“Cody was there: this long, lanky kid who kept hitting triples. And these fields are big out here in Arizona. On those big fields, all he did was hit one-hoppers or balls off the center field and left-center field walls. He didn’t really pull balls, and that’s what he did. He was amazing. Through minor league ball, he was doing the same thing.”
With Franklin, Bellinger was a lean, doubles machine with a great arm and good defense. Suddenly, after his MLB debut, he didn’t look like that same player.
“He started pulling the ball in his rookie year, went to the major leagues, and then stayed in LA,” Franklin said. “And I’m not gonna say the Dodgers messed him up. Well, I will say they messed him up, but I will also say they made him into an MVP. So you’ve got to give them credit for that, too.”
As Bellinger’s approach evolved toward pulling the baseball, he became yet another pull-happy, homer-hungry slugger who thrived in The Show — an archetype fans are used to in modern baseball.
Franklin knew better.
“When they worked with him, they had him go from hitting the ball the other way to learning how to pull the ball better because he got older, and that’s what naturally happens. Well, guess what? When you stop working on the other stuff and only work on the drills that are helping you pull in the air, you eventually start continuing to pull, continuing to pull, continuing to pull, and guess what? You forget the other stuff, and you don’t even know how to go back to it anymore.”
Bellinger knew what he wanted to do. He’d done it for years. He had the natural juice to hit baseballs very far. But in those deep counts, or contact situations, his new approach took over. He couldn’t find the same swing that once landed him on Franklin’s D-backs scout team.
“Boom! It didn’t work,” Franklin exclaimed.
“So now he’s texting during the season. I think it was the 2020 season, showing me BP on the field, doing all this other stuff. We didn’t have the drills. We didn’t have anything for him to understand because he didn’t have a foundation. He lost his foundation. So at that point, now whoa, oops, he gets non-tendered.”
From MVP to clutter, cast away from the same city he helped to a world championship, Bellinger had hit rock bottom. At a wedding, surrounded by other big leaguers, his career was reborn.
“So at that point, we’re at Jamie Westbrook’s wedding,” Franklin recalled.
Westbrook is another one of Franklin’s pupils, who had a brief stint with the Boston Red Sox in 2024.
“Pat Murphy was there, and Bobby Dalbec. All these guys get DFA’d or non-tendered. It was really interesting. You can imagine. There was a lot of drinking going on since they just got let go. So we’re like, ‘Hey, let’s go hit.’”
Those three words — “Let’s go hit” — may have saved Bellinger’s career. But it literally took baby steps.
“At the start, we didn’t hit. All we did was learn how to step back to the pitcher again, straight, because he couldn’t keep a ball fair. I mean, he opened up so badly that anytime he hit a ball hard, it would either go foul or to the first baseman. It was disastrous, as we know. Everyone saw it. So, we learned how to step. Then we learned how to keep our direction with a swing. Then we learned how to keep our direction while hitting the ball at 50 miles an hour.”
“People don’t understand,” Franklin continued. “They come here, and I tell them to try to hit a ball at 50 mph, but they can’t. High school kids, college kids can’t. I’m like, ‘Dude, how hard is this?’”
Through rigorous trial and error, Franklin and Bellinger developed a process that worked. At times, however, it took some mental manipulation.
“Cody’s such a late starter; it’s unbelievable,” Franklin said. “Well, everyone’s like, ‘All right, Micah, you need to tell him to start earlier!’ Well, that’s like a four-letter word to him. He can’t. We’re like, ‘Don’t you think if he could start earlier, he would?’”
Franklin used drills that positioned Bellinger’s body so he had to start earlier. As the body matures and becomes stronger, more ways exist to compensate for a lack of mechanical intuition. Bellinger is a strong professional athlete, so it was necessary to keep him within a controlled environment while making such finite adjustments.
“We had to figure out different drills where he’s starting earlier and doesn’t even know it, because his body is getting to an autonomous state,” Franklin said. “So we put a foam roller on him, so he just rolls. You know, when you roll your back out or roll your leg out or whatever. So we put that on his foot, and he has to roll earlier. We also used a ball. So it was drills like that, while making sure he maintained his direction; those were huge. Not pulling the ball, just staying up the middle or the other way, just like he did back in high school. We had to find his old self somewhere in his memory.”
Bellinger’s process included two-to-three-hour cage sessions where Franklin said they’d hit the ball only 90 to 110 times. The cycle was swing, talk, adjust, repeat.
After that, Bellinger signed a one-year prove-it deal with the Chicago Cubs ahead of the 2023 season.
He played two great years in Chicago, and then headed for the Bronx, where he’s now in the midst of a newly inked five-year, $162.5 million deal that’ll keep him in pinstripes through 2030 (barring opt-outs).
In the four years since Bellinger was ousted from Hollywood, he’s back on the big screen. His Silver Slugger in 2023 and most recent All-Star selection in 2026 have all but cemented a comeback that’s nothing short of remarkable.
During this recent success, Bellinger has become less of a good power hitter and more of a good hitter with power – like a fellow Yankee legend.
“When I wrote this down way back when I did a scouting report in high school, I said he’s very much more like a Paul O’Neill hitter,” said Franklin. “That’s who he is right now versus the guy that’s an MVP hitting balls way, way out. That’s just not him. Especially at the age he’s at now.”
Bellinger may have started his career as one kind of player, but it wasn’t who he was at his core. Franklin knew, the baseball Gods knew, and even Bellinger himself may have known.
Still, few outfielders impact a game the way Bellinger can, and the stats matured alongside his approach.
This season, Bellinger ranks in the 81st percentile in batting run value and is an elite defender across the board. It took time to re-establish what he once was, but his 9.7 bWAR (and counting) across the past two seasons is profoundly consistent and can only be rivaled by stardom.
Franklin played professional baseball from 1990 through 2004. He traveled to chase his dreams and never found an environment he couldn’t hit in.
Baseball, the game of storytelling, still feels the vibrations of Franklin’s pro career, if not through the might of his own swing, then through the knowledge he’s weaponized to create some of baseball’s best hitters.
Other MLB stars who have put in work in Franklin’s cage include Matt Chapman, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Nationals’ superstar James Wood.
Baseball is a paradoxical game that can’t be understood through one lens, but Franklin’s approach and his athletes’ hard work made a star reborn.
Franklin is still in the cage, day in and day out, shaping the next generation of hitters, and he knows all too well, as does Bellinger, that baseball is a game where you’ll never be perfect.
“In baseball, you can’t put the person in the perfect position; you need to put them in the most efficient position.”

item.content:encoded:
Aunque no ganaba un juego desde el 27 de abril, Max Fried tiene una efectividad de 1.83 con 50 ponches en 44.1 entradas después del receso del Juego de Estrellas. (Abbie Parr)
Por The Associated Press
Agencia de noticias
Minneapolis - Max Fried consiguió su primera victoria desde el 27 de abril, respaldado por jonrones de Cody Bellinger y Spencer Jones que ayudaron a los Yankees de Nueva York a mantenerse en la pelea por el Este de la Liga Americana con un triunfo el martes 8-1 sobre los Twins de Minnesota.
Fried (5-4) permitió una carrera en siete sólidas entradas y 88 lanzamientos, en su apertura más duradera en casi cinco meses, para asegurar que los Yankees (88-63) se mantuvieran a 3.5 juegos de Tampa Bay (91-59) en la lucha por el liderato divisional.
Los Yankees, que aseguraron al menos un puesto de comodín el lunes, necesitarán que Fried mantenga este nivel en la postemporada.
Fried, quien pasó 71 juegos en la lista de lesionados en dos periodos por una contusión ósea en el codo, tiene una efectividad de 1.83 con 50 ponches en 44.1 entradas en nueve aperturas después del receso del Juego de Estrellas.
Bellinger, que conectó tres hits y recibió una base por bolas, puso en marcha rápidamente a los Yankees con su decimosexto cuadrangular, un batazo de dos carreras después de que Ben Rice abrió el juego con un sencillo ante Bailey Ober (7-6). Bellinger batea para .377 (26 de 69) en sus últimos 17 juegos.
Jones conectó su décimo jonrón con dos salidas en la sexta, un cuadrangular de tres carreras ante Taylor Rogers. Un error defensivo del campocorto novato Kaelen Culpepper hizo que las cuatro carreras del episodio fueran sucias.
Nueva York tiene 11 jugadores con 10 o más jonrones esta temporada.
La estrella del jardín derecho Aaron Judge, que busca recuperar su forma tras regresar recientemente de una costilla rota, se quedó en la banca para descansar mientras los Yankees acumulaban 14 hits.

item.title: [New York Post] Every playoff run requires unlikely heroes — and the Yankees’ roster is filled with options
item.dc:creator: Andrew Crane
item.description: When the champagne celebration ended Monday night, after the Yankees removed their goggles and the booze-filled plastic coverings protecting the visitors’ clubhouse at Target Field were taken down, some of their postseason certainties were starting to take shape. item.content:encoded:
When the champagne celebration ended Monday night, after the Yankees removed their goggles and the booze-filled plastic coverings protecting the visitors’ clubhouse at Target Field were taken down, some of their postseason certainties were starting to take shape.
They, after the Blue Jays lost, had clinched a spot in the tournament. Barring a collapse by the Rays over the final two weeks, the Yankees will start from a wild-card position. Barring a collapse by their own roster, they’ll occupy the top wild-card spot. And barring any last-minute nightmares, Aaron Judge, with his home run Monday as evidence, Max Fried, who’s trying to rediscover his vintage form (as he did in Tuesday’s 8-1 win over the Twins), Gerrit Cole, who’s trying to figure out why he’s letting up all these home runs and Cam Schlittler, in the midst of strengthening his case for the American League Cy Young Award, are all healthy.
But in a year where the Yankees kept needing to navigate injuries, where star after star after star kept missing time, unlikely heroes materialized. And if this group ends up being the one to snap the World Series title drought that dates back to 2009, those names — from Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn to second-half Austin Wells and José Caballero — will need to contribute.
Every contender has its stars. The Judges. The Coles. The Schlittlers, as well as the Frieds, the Ben Rices, the David Bednars and the Cody Bellingers. The constants expected to anchor the run. The faces who’ve been on that October stage before.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Aaron Boone Admite Que Spencer Jones Echó Por Tierra El Plan Original De Los Yankees Para El Bateador Novato
item.dc:creator: Sara Molnick

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Durante dos noches seguidas, los Yankees han sumado siete carreras con el mismo golpe. Aaron Judge conectó un jonrón de tres carreras el lunes. Veinticuatro horas después, Spencer Jones lo repitió ante un rival del que Nueva York intentó protegerlo en su momento.
Jones conectó un lanzamiento «sweeper» 2-2 del zurdo de los Twins, Taylor Rogers, en la sexta entrada del martes y lo mandó a 423 pies, justo al centro del campo. Ese jonrón de tres carreras dio a los Yankees una ventaja de 7-1 en lo que acabó siendo una victoria por 8-1 en el Target Field.
El enfrentamiento hizo que el swing resultara más revelador que la distancia. Rogers se había enfrentado a 133 bateadores zurdos esta temporada sin permitir ningún jonrón antes de que el novato de los Yankees rompiera esa racha. Jones había fallado una serie de lanzamientos rasantes antes de conectar otro por el centro y mandarlo fuera a 108 mph.
Cody Bellinger ya había dado a los Yankees una ventaja de 2-0 en la primera entrada con su decimosexto jonrón, mientras que Max Fried lanzó siete entradas cediendo solo una carrera. Los Yankees terminaron con 14 hits —todos los titulares consiguieron al menos uno—, mejoraron su balance a 88-63 y ganaron por séptima vez en ocho partidos.
El jonrón de Jones fue el décimo, lo que le convierte en el undécimo jugador de los Yankees en alcanzar las dos cifras esta temporada, la cifra más alta del club desde 2019.
Su poder había estado un poco apagado durante casi dos semanas, pero su bate no. Jones bateó .333 durante esa racha de 11 partidos sin jonrones. En sus últimos 25 partidos, ha conectado 28 de 81, con un promedio de .346, 10 hits de más de una base, cinco jonrones, 19 carreras impulsadas, 17 carreras anotadas y un OPS de .993.
Cada vez es más difícil pasar por alto la curva de crecimiento
Las estadísticas de Jones esta temporada, .259/.331/.452, no reflejan lo mucho que ha cambiado su perfil en los Yankees. Empezó mayo con un promedio de .167/.259/.167 en 10 partidos, subió a .255/.340/.468 en junio y alcanzó un slugging de .611 en ocho partidos de julio. En agosto registró unas estadísticas de .239/.290/.446, pero en septiembre ha logrado un .340/.415/.532 en 13 partidos.
La tendencia general de la segunda mitad de la temporada es parecida. El novato de los Yankees ha bateado .271/.337/.490 desde el parón del All-Star, tras registrar .233/.317/.370 antes de él. Lo ha conseguido mientras jugaba habitualmente en el centro del campo y seguía trabajando para superar los problemas con los strikeouts que le han perseguido desde las ligas menores.
El exentrenador de los Yankees, Joe Girardi, destacó el alcance de esa mejora antes del partido del lunes. Girardi señaló los ajustes de Jones con corredores en posición de anotar, su capacidad para atrapar lanzamientos a gran velocidad, su defensa, su velocidad en las bases y la potencia de su brazo.
«Es capaz de hacerlo todo», dijo Girardi.
Bellinger, que comparte el jardín de los Yankees con Jones, dijo que el cambio va más allá de los resultados. Destacó lo tranquilo que se ve el novato, independientemente de quién esté lanzando.
«Ha sido increíble. Es decir, su swing es… es un swing realmente bueno, y mentalmente entiende lo que quiere hacer contra [los zurdos] y sabe lo que tiene que hacer frente a ellos», dijo Bellinger. «Da igual si el lanzador es diestro o zurdo, no parece que le afecte. Tiene un buen enfoque».
Jones le ha dado la vuelta al tema de los turnos
Las cifras explican por qué la estrategia inicial de los Yankees ya no encaja. Jones ha tenido 51 turnos al bate contra lanzadores zurdos y batea con un promedio de .435, un porcentaje de embasado de .490 y un porcentaje de slugging de .761, lo que le da un OPS de 1,251. Tiene 20 hits en 46 turnos al bate, incluyendo tres jonrones y 12 carreras impulsadas.
Entre los bateadores de la MLB con al menos 50 turnos al bate contra lanzadores zurdos, tanto su promedio de bateo como su OPS ocupan el primer puesto. Es algo inusual para un novato de los Yankees que llegó a las Grandes Ligas con dudas sobre su capacidad para evitar los strikes y al que, al principio, se le dosificaba con cuidado en los enfrentamientos contra lanzadores del mismo lado.
Además, los enfrentamientos contra lanzadores diestros representan una parte desproporcionada de su rendimiento. Jones suma 59 hits, 10 jonrones y 37 carreras impulsadas en un total de 78 partidos. Según un cálculo de PinstripesNation, solo alrededor del 20 % de sus turnos al bate han sido contra lanzadores zurdos, pero esos enfrentamientos suponen aproximadamente el 34 % de sus hits, el 30 % de sus jonrones y el 32 % de sus carreras impulsadas.
En sus últimos 32 turnos al bate, el jardinero de los Yankees tiene un promedio de bateo de .317, un OPS de .900, un porcentaje de slugging de .532 y cinco jonrones. Los Yankees también estaban pendientes de si la calidad de sus turnos al bate se mantenía incluso cuando el swing de jonrón desaparecía temporalmente.
Esas cifras han cambiado la forma en que el entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, lo maneja. A principios de temporada, Boone intentó facilitar la adaptación del novato zurdo a la vida en las Grandes Ligas limitando su exposición frente a lanzadores zurdos. Más de cuatro meses después, esa protección ha desaparecido prácticamente por completo.
«Le estaba ayudando a adaptarse poco a poco. Y la verdad es que ha irrumpido con fuerza», dijo Boone con una risita. «Además, se ha enfrentado a muchos lanzadores zurdos difíciles y, la verdad, creo que ha sabido controlar sus turnos al bate, lo cual es genial de ver».
Puede que la duda sobre la alineación de octubre ya se esté resolviendo sola
Antes, los Yankees tenían una razón muy clara para proteger a Jones de los zurdos. Ahora ya no. Su rendimiento contra los zurdos se ha convertido en uno de sus puntos fuertes, lo que elimina la razón basada en el emparejamiento para dejarlo en el banquillo cuando, en octubre, los bullpens empiezan a recurrir a especialistas.
Esto es importante porque la situación en el centro del campo ha cambiado rápidamente. Trent Grisham ha bateado .211/.308/.395 en 121 partidos, mientras que Jones ha pasado de tener un papel esporádico en los Yankees a ser titular a medida que la lucha por los playoffs se va ajustando. Su capacidad para mantenerse en la alineación tanto contra lanzadores diestros como zurdos le da a Boone más libertad a la hora de manejar a Bellinger, Heliot Ramos y el resto de la plantilla.
Los Yankees aún tienen que decidir cómo encajan todas las piezas cuando la plantilla esté al completo. Jones ha simplificado mucho una parte de ese debate. Lo que en mayo era un punto débil que Boone intentó gestionar, ahora parece un enfrentamiento que los rivales tendrán que tener en cuenta en octubre.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario abajo.

item.title: [pinstripesnation.com] La Goleada De Los Yankees Por 8-1 A Los Twins Pone De Manifiesto El Crucial Ajuste En Los Lanzamientos Lentos De Max Fried Y Su Enorme Salto De Calidad De Cara A Los Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Esteban Quiñones
item.description: MINNEAPOLIS — Apenas se había secado el champán cuando los Yankees se enfrentaron a la pregunta que quedaba pendiente desde la noche anterior: ¿Aparecería sin energía un equipo que se había pasado la noche de fiesta hasta altas horas de la madrugada? Pues no fue así. item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Apenas se había secado el champán cuando los Yankees se enfrentaron a la pregunta que quedaba pendiente desde la noche anterior: ¿Aparecería sin energía un equipo que se había pasado la noche de fiesta hasta altas horas de la madrugada?
Pues no fue así.
Cody Bellinger conectó un jonrón de dos carreras en la primera entrada; los Yankees terminaron con 14 hits —cada titular consiguió al menos uno— y Nueva York nunca estuvo por detrás en el marcador en la victoria por 8-1 sobre los Twins en el Target Field el martes.
Pero la cifra que más importaba para los Yankees en octubre era el número de lanzamientos de Max Fried.
Tras una salida en la que le costó mucho completar 3 1/3 entradas contra Colorado, Fried lanzó siete entradas con 88 lanzamientos, cediendo una carrera y seis hits, con seis strikeouts y ninguna base por bolas. Fue su salida más larga desde el 22 de abril y su primera victoria desde el 27 de abril. En Colorado, el lanzador de los Yankees necesitó 80 lanzamientos para conseguir 10 outs. El martes, solo necesitó ocho más para lograr 21.
Fried dijo que un pequeño ajuste en el control de sus lanzamientos lentos lo cambió todo.
Cómo los Yankees sentenciaron el partido desde el principio
Después de que Dean Kremer les limitara a dos hits, los Yankees se lanzaron a por Bailey Ober. Ben Rice, tras estar a punto de recibir un pelotazo, abrió la entrada con un sencillo. Bellinger le siguió con su decimosexto jonrón al centro-derecha.
Bellinger conectó 3 de 4 con una base por bolas y lleva un promedio de bateo de 0,377 en sus últimos 17 partidos, con cinco jonrones desde que volvió tras una lesión en el tendón de la corva. El promedio del bateador de los Yankees subió a 0,272, su mejor marca desde el 22 de junio.
Anthony Volpe y Ali Sánchez conectaron dos sencillos seguidos en la segunda entrada, pero Ober dejó a ambos en base. Minnesota respondió cuando Royce Lewis llegó a base con un sencillo al cuadro, robó la segunda y anotó gracias a un sencillo impulsor de Emmanuel Rodríguez con dos outs. Fried zanjó la jugada con un pickoff de libro contra Rodríguez.
Los Yankees respondieron en la tercera entrada. Heliot Ramos consiguió una base por bolas, Luis García Jr. conectó un sencillo y George Lombard Jr. bateó un sencillo impulsador con dos outs por la banda derecha, poniendo el marcador 3-1 a su favor. Volpe consiguió otra base por bolas y llenó las bases, pero el batazo de Sánchez al centro se quedó en la zona de advertencia.
Ober repartió nueve hits a lo largo de 5 1/3 entradas y encajó tres carreras, mientras Nueva York dejaba a sus corredores en las bases una y otra vez. Eso cambió en la sexta.
Rice llegó a base por un error del campocorto Kaelen Culpepper, Bellinger consiguió una base por bolas tras cuatro lanzamientos y Ramos conectó un doble ante el zurdo Taylor Rogers para poner el 4-1 en el marcador.
Le tocó el turno a Spencer Jones. Tras fallar una serie de lanzamientos bajos y lentos, el bateador novato de los Yankees conectó el cuarto, que le llegó justo por el centro con una cuenta de 2-2, y lo mandó 423 pies al centro para un jonrón de tres carreras, poniendo el marcador 7-1.
Rogers no había cedido ningún jonrón a un bateador zurdo en toda la temporada, en 133 turnos al bate. Jones puso fin a esa racha. Ahora tiene un promedio de bateo de .435/.490/.761 contra lanzadores zurdos y se ha convertido en el undécimo Yankee con más de diez jonrones esta temporada, igualando el total del club en 2019.
Las cuatro carreras de la sexta entrada fueron sucias debido a un error de Culpepper.
Nueva York sumó una carrera en la novena entrada cuando Lombard consiguió una base por bolas, avanzó gracias a un roletazo de out y anotó gracias al sencillo de José Caballero ante Andrew Morris.
Todos los titulares de los Yankees consiguieron al menos un hit y llegaron a base. Ramos, Lombard y Volpe llegaron a base tres veces cada uno. Con esta victoria, Nueva York queda con un balance de 88-63, tras encadenar siete victorias en ocho partidos y con una ventaja de seis partidos sobre Boston en la lucha por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
El ajuste que hizo Fried entre sus salidas
Fried dijo que un mejor control de sus lanzamientos lentos le permitió utilizarlos en cualquier cuenta.
«Simplemente tuve más control sobre mis lanzamientos lentos. Pude lanzarlos para conseguir strikes. Siento que he podido lanzarlos en cualquier cuenta. Y tenía mucha, mucha confianza en eso. He trabajado muy bien con Ali (Sánchez) y, además, cuando tienes a la defensa haciendo grandes jugadas detrás de ti, eso te da más confianza», le dijo el as de los Yankees a Meredith Marakovits, de YES Network.
Era la novena salida de Fried desde que volvió tras su segunda baja por lesión, a causa de un hematoma óseo en el codo izquierdo. El objetivo de los Yankees era reducir el número de lanzamientos por entrada y que aguantara más tiempo en el montículo.
«La verdad es que me ha venido muy bien poder hacer lo que me ha parecido una salida completa, sin estar tan limitado por el recuento de lanzamientos», dijo Fried. «Aún así, llegué a los 88 lanzamientos y terminé la séptima entrada, así que me alegro de haber podido tachar eso de la lista. Pero es una mezcla de sentirme bien con dónde estamos y, al mismo tiempo, saber que todavía tenemos cosas en las que trabajar».
El entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, dijo que Fried podría mejorar aún más la próxima vez.
«Me gusta cómo está ahora, y espero que pueda seguir mejorando un poco más en el próximo partido y que siga así», dijo Boone. «Pero me ha encantado cómo ha atacado la zona de strike, cómo ha controlado los conteos y cómo ha tenido mucha presencia con la mayoría de sus lanzamientos esta noche».
¿Por qué es importante el momento en octubre?
La salud y la carga de trabajo de Fried son clave para las cuentas de los Yankees de cara a la postemporadahttps://pinstripesnation.com/mlb-2026-postseason-schedule-yankees-2026-08-11/. Tras el partido del martes, tenía una efectividad de 2,63 y, desde el parón del All-Star, acumula una efectividad de 1,83 con 50 strikeouts en 44 1/3 entradas en nueve partidos como titular.
Los datos sobre los lanzamientos coinciden. Según un gráfico de Pitch Profiler, Fried lanzó su «sweeper» 19 veces, lo que supone el 21,6 % de sus 88 lanzamientos. Los bateadores fallaron el golpe en el 70 % de las ocasiones y obtuvieron un promedio de embasado ponderado esperado de 0,098.
Su bola curva, lanzada 15 veces, generó un porcentaje de fallos del 33,3 %. El cambio de velocidad del as de los Yankees , lanzado 13 veces, generó un porcentaje de fallos del 37,5 % y un promedio esperado de .175.
Esos tres lanzamientos lentos supusieron 47 de sus 88 lanzamientos, más de la mitad de su carga de trabajo. Esa confianza en sus lanzamientos secundarios le ayudó a conseguir una tasa global de strikes fallidos del 32,6 %, sin conceder bases por bolas. La bola rápida de cuatro costuras y la sinker de la estrella de los Yankees le dieron los peores resultados, y fueron los que menos utilizó.
Ahora viene una prueba más dura.
Fried se enfrentará a los Rays la semana que viene en uno de los dos partidos de una doble jornada que dará inicio a una serie decisiva de cuatro partidos en el Yankee Stadium. Los Yankees siguen a 3 1/2 partidos del Tampa Bay (91-59) en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 11 partidos por disputar.
«Va a ser béisbol de eliminatorias», dijo Fried. «Son dos equipos, dos equipos realmente buenos, que van a darlo todo. Estoy deseando formar parte de esto y no veo la hora de que llegue la semana que viene».
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.content:encoded:
Our Standards: The Thomson Reuters Trust Principles.
September 16 - Spencer Jones belted a three-run home run, Cody Bellinger hammered a two-run shot, and the New York Yankees cruised to an 8-1 win over the Minnesota Twins on Tuesday in Minneapolis.
Bellinger collected three hits while Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Anthony Volpe had two apiece for New York (88-63), which earned its third win in a row and its seventh in eight games. The Yankees will look to complete a three-game sweep of the Twins on Wednesday afternoon.
Luke Keaschall went 3-for-4 and Emmanuel Rodriguez finished 2-for-3 with an RBI for Minnesota (70-81), which took its seventh loss in nine games.
Yankees left-hander Max Fried (5-4) allowed one run on six hits in seven innings. He walked none and struck out six.
Twins right-hander Bailey Ober (7-6) gave up three runs on nine hits in 5 1/3 innings. He fanned three and walked two.
The Yankees jumped to a 2-0 lead in the top of the first. Ben Rice hit a leadoff single, and Bellinger followed with a 399-foot, two-run homer over the wall in right-center field.
The Twins cut the deficit to 2-1 in the second. Royce Lewis reached on an infield single, swiped second base and scored on a single to center by Rodriguez.
Lombard put the Yankees on top 3-1 in the third with an RBI single to right.
New York broke the game open with four runs in the sixth.
Rice reached on an error, Bellinger walked and Ramos drove in Rice with a double to left.
Two batters later, Jones belted a three-run homer to center to put New York up by six runs. The 423-foot blast landed in the second deck of the outfield.
The Yankees capped the scoring in the ninth when Jose Caballero singled to center to score Lombard from second.
New York left-hander Ryan Yarbrough finished the game with two scoreless innings. He threw 21 of 29 pitches for strikes.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Baltimore, Maryland.- Paul Goldschmidt conectó un jonrón en el primer lanzamiento del partido, Trent Grisham bateó un cuadrangular de tres carreras y los Yankees de Nueva York vencieron a los Orioles de Baltimore 6-2 el martes por la noche para poner fin a una racha de cuatro derrotas consecutivas.
Will Warren (5-1) permitió dos carreras y cuatro hits en 5 2/3 entradas para los Yankees. Fue una buena actuación para el lanzador derecho, quien había permitido seis carreras en cuatro entradas a Texas en su apertura anterior.
El cuarto jonrón de apertura de Goldschmidt en su carrera y el segundo en cuatro días puso a Nueva York al frente definitivamente, y el batazo de Grisham puso el marcador 6-0 en la tercera entrada. Ambos jonrones fueron contra el zurdo Trevor Rogers, quien solo duró cuatro entradas en su regreso de la lista de lesionados tras una larga enfermedad.
En su primer partido como lanzador desde el 25 de abril, Rogers (2-4) permitió seis carreras y seis hits, elevando su efectividad a 5.77 en comparación con 1.81 en 2025.
Rogers se metió en problemas en la tercera entrada cuando otorgó dos bases por bolas consecutivas que llenaron las bases con un out. Luego, Cody Bellinger bateó un rodado que resultó en un out forzado, produciendo una carrera; Amed Rosario impulsó una carrera con un sencillo al cuadro y Grisham coronó la remontada con su sexto jonrón.
Esa ofensiva fue más que suficiente para asegurar a Nueva York su décima victoria en 11 partidos contra Baltimore, remontándonos a la temporada pasada.
Los equipos lograron superar las cuatro revisiones de decisiones arbitrales que presentaron ante el árbitro principal, Hunter Wendelstedt.
Los Yankees de Nueva York llamaron al campocorto Anthony Volpe de la filial Triple-A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre y colocaron a José Caballero en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por una fractura en un dedo. Se espera que Volpe sea titular en el último partido de la serie el miércoles.
A continuación
El partido del miércoles se adelantó a las 13:05 h desde las 18:35 h debido a la amenaza de mal tiempo. Max Fried (4-2, 2.91 ERA) será el abridor por Nueva York, y Kyle Bradish (1-5, 4.83) será el probable abridor por Baltimore.
Información: AP.

item.title: [New York Post] Aaron Boone has injury-plagued Yankees back in the playoffs with bigger goals in mind
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — When the Yankees wrapped up their spot in the postseason Monday night, Aaron Boone joined some select company.
He became the second manager in MLB history to reach the postseason in at least eight of his first nine seasons, joining Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, who has now done it in each of his first 11 seasons. Boone is also the third manager to make the playoffs in eight of his first nine seasons with the Yankees, joining Joe Torre and Casey Stengel.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Of course, Roberts, Torre and Stengel have combined to win 14 World Series titles while Boone is still in search of his first. And ultimately, in New York, that is how he will be judged, as opposed to just getting his team to the postseason regularly.
But in a season in which the Yankees have had most of their biggest stars spend sizable chunks of time on the injured list, Boone has helped lead them through the adversity to still have as good a chance as any team in the American League to make a run to the World Series.
“He’s our guy,” Aaron Judge said in the champagne-soaked visitors clubhouse at Target Field late Monday night. “He’s the one we go to battle for every single night and just lucky and blessed to have him here, to be able to fight for a guy like that. He loves every single guy in this room and we’re going to fight till the end for him.”
The Yankees still have bigger things left to accomplish this year, starting with trying to chase down the Rays for the division, but then more importantly, attempting to go the distance in October for the first time since 2009.
But by the time they clinched their playoff spot, the Yankees had survived 84 games without Judge; 124 games and counting without Giancarlo Stanton; 25 games without Cody Bellinger; 27 games and counting without Trent Grisham (across two IL stints); 22 games without Ryan McMahon (across two IL stints); 51 games without Gerrit Cole; 71 games without Max Fried (across two IL stints); 40 games without Carlos Rodón (across two IL stints); 21 games and counting without Ryan Weathers; and 150 games and counting without Clarke Schmidt, among others.
Every team deals with injuries, but not every team survives them to the extent that the Yankees have, entering Tuesday on pace to match the 94 wins they have had in each of the last two seasons.
“It’s very tough for a Yankee manager to win Manager of the Year,” bench coach Brad Ausmus said Tuesday, pointing to the high expectations with which the franchise enters every season. “Obviously [Rays manager] Kevin Cash and [White Sox manager] Will Venable will be extremely strong candidates. But with the job [Boone] has done this year with the injuries, keeping the group as one cohesive unit, I think he should definitely be in the discussion.”
There were some rough stretches along the way during Judge’s three-month absence, most notably a 5-15 skid from late June to early July.
Shop Yankees Merch
Even when the Yankees started to snap out of that, it did not often feel like it as their offense was still in a malaise and almost every game they played was a low-scoring, nail-biting battle.
Though that stretch threatens to ultimately cost the Yankees a chance at overtaking the Rays for the AL East, Boone is hoping he will have his team in a position to be at its best in the postseason to make a run at an elusive title.
“It’s not easy,” Austin Wells said. “You lose guys left and right at different parts of the season. Having to piece wins together, keep us right there in the division race throughout the whole year, he does an impressive job. Definitely a testament to him. Looking forward to more of that, more winning decisions and keep leading us.”
